---
title: "File-backed data and GWAS"
description: "Stream screening from packed genotypes and large assay matrices."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>',message=FALSE,warning=FALSE)
```

`l0glmData()` separates matrix storage from model selection. SIS/ISIS reads
predictors in bounded blocks, then L0glm fits the retained working design using
its ordinary or special-family engine. The original predictor count determines
the GIC preset and score, and returned coefficients retain the original sparse
dimensions. This works with Gaussian and other GLMs, negative binomial,
multinomial and Cox models, including weights and offsets.

## One interface for large matrices

```{r source}
library(L0glm)
set.seed(18)
X <- matrix(rnorm(100*2000),100,2000)
y <- 2*X[,1]-2*X[,2]+rnorm(100)
source <- l0glmData(X,control=list(block.cells=20000,max.cells=30000))
fit <- l0glmFit(source,y,screen='SIS',nsis=20L,lambda='gic')
coef(fit)[which(Matrix::rowSums(coef(fit)!=0)>0),,drop=FALSE]
```

For a large file, replace the constructor while keeping the model call:

```{r backends, eval=FALSE}
genotype <- l0glmData('genotypes.bed',n=4000L,p=1733480L)
fit <- l0glmFit(genotype,case_status,family=binomial(),screen='SIS',nsis=1000L)

assay <- l0glmData('cells.h5ad',dataset='counts')
fit <- l0glmFit(assay,response,family=poisson())

assay <- l0glmData('cells.h5seurat',dataset='assays/RNA/counts')
assay <- l0glmData('cells.loom')
source <- l0glmData(bigmemory::attach.big.matrix('matrix.desc'))
```

H5AD, h5Seurat and loom adapters put observations in rows and genes in columns.
Generic HDF5 datasets retain their supplied orientation; `transpose` can be set
explicitly. Sparse HDF5/DelayedArray assays retain sparse working blocks.
HDF5Array, DelayedArray, rhdf5 and bigmemory are optional dependencies.

Double-precision bigmemory designs are screened directly through their existing
native mapping, using read-only access. Each OpenMP worker reads its assigned columns
without first copying them into an R matrix. Subsets retain the original row
and column indices, and screening statistics and tie handling match resident
matrices. Other storage types and mean-imputed data use bounded column blocks.

Subsetting with `drop=FALSE` creates a view. `as.matrix()` makes an explicit
bounded read. An unscreened working design, the retained fit matrix and requested
outputs must fit the configurable `max.cells` guard. Full-design IRLS on an
arbitrarily large tall matrix still requires a dedicated streamed solver; the
current interface keeps that memory requirement explicit. For plain LASSO,
the native biglasso adapter below can fit a complete double bigmemory design.

## One million predictors on disk

The resident example uses 1,000 observations and 60 nonzero effects. With
`l0glmData()` the same Gaussian construction can be extended to **10,000
observations and one million predictors**, while generating and reading the
design in bounded blocks. A double-precision backing file occupies **80 GB**;
the active fitting problem is much smaller.

Run the following from an empty working directory with enough disk space.
Only a block of 256 predictor columns is generated at a time. The random
number sequence matches `matrix(rnorm(as.double(n)*p), n, p)`.

```{r million-file, eval=FALSE}
library(L0glm)
library(bigmemory)
RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1L)
n <- 10000L
p <- 1000000L
backing <- filebacked.big.matrix(nrow=n,ncol=p,type="double",
  backingfile="normal.bin",descriptorfile="normal.desc",backingpath=getwd())
set.seed(123)
for(first in seq.int(1L,p,by=256L)) {
  j <- seq.int(first,min(p,first+255L))
  backing[,j] <- matrix(rnorm(as.double(n)*length(j)),n)
}
active <- sample.int(p,60L)
beta <- numeric(p)
beta[active] <- runif(60L,-.8,.8)
set.seed(1)
y <- drop(backing[,active,drop=FALSE]%*%beta[active])+rnorm(n)

# The descriptor can be reattached in a new R session.
training <- seq_len(8000L)
test <- 8001:10000
X <- l0glmData(attach.big.matrix("normal.desc"),control=list(
  block.columns=4096L,block.cells=length(training)*4096,max.cells=1e8))
system.time(fit <- l0glmFit(X[training,,drop=FALSE],y[training],
  family=gaussian(),intercept=TRUE,screen="ISIS",screen.nthreads=8L))
l0glmMetrics(fit,beta_true=beta)[
  c("gic","TP","FP","FN","TN","F1_score","MCC")]
sqrt(mean((predict(fit,X[test,,drop=FALSE])-y[test])^2))
```

<!-- BEGIN file-normal-metrics -->
| Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | TN | F1 | MCC | Test RMSE |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1695.53 | 24652 | 50 | 1 | 10 | 999939 | 0.901 | 0.904 | 0.993 |

Generating the 80 GB file took **488.31 seconds**, excluded from the fitting time.
<!-- END file-normal-metrics -->

The first 8,000 rows are used for screening and fitting, and the remaining
2,000 rows assess prediction. The model includes a free intercept and uses
4,096-column streaming blocks. The GIC preset uses the original one million
predictors. Generation and fitting times are recorded separately. The
[complete reproduction script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_filebacked_normal.R)
creates a reusable descriptor and response cache and reports the screening
history. The response, truth and descriptor should be saved together when
continuing in a new session.

### Compare with native file-backed LASSO

The optional [biglasso](https://pbreheny.github.io/biglasso/) solver fits plain
LASSO directly on the same backing file. Its native row-index interface also
reuses the file across cross-validation folds. `screen="none"` keeps all
predictors available; biglasso still uses its own screening rules to accelerate
the convex LASSO path. The shared `sparseGLM()` interface selects lambda using
the same likelihood and information-criterion code as the other methods.

```{r biglasso, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("biglasso") # once
comparison <- sparseGLM(X[training,,drop=FALSE],y[training],family=gaussian(),
  method="biglasso",screen="none",intercept=TRUE,tune="bic",nlambda=10L,
  options=list(ncores=8L,lambda.min=.05),beta_true=beta)
l0glmMetrics(comparison)[c("method","seconds","gic","TP","FP","F1_score","MCC")]
sqrt(mean((predict(comparison,X[test,,drop=FALSE])[[1]]-y[test])^2))

# The same file supports training-row cross-validation without dense copies.
cv <- sparseGLM(X[training,,drop=FALSE],y[training],family=gaussian(),
  method="biglasso",screen="none",intercept=TRUE,tune="cv",nfolds=5L,
  nlambda=10L,options=list(ncores=8L,lambda.min=.05))
```

Biglasso includes a free Gaussian/logistic intercept. For a matched comparison,
give both methods a free intercept. The reproduction script uses a GIC preset
and ISIS for L0glm, while LASSO selects from ten native lambda values using BIC. Both models
train on 8,000 rows and predict the same held-out 2,000 rows. The L0glm streaming
blocks contain up to 4,096 columns; the native LASSO solver reads the backing
matrix directly. Neither method copies the full design into an R matrix.

<!-- BEGIN file-lasso-metrics -->
| Method | Selection | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | F1 | MCC | Test RMSE |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| L0glm | GIC preset | 1695.53 | 24652 | 50 | 1 | 10 | 0.901 | 0.904 | 0.993 |
| biglasso LASSO | BIC path | 792.32 | 25933 | 51 | 3 | 9 | 0.895 | 0.896 | 1.074 |
<!-- END file-lasso-metrics -->

Biglasso finishes the full-predictor LASSO path in **13.2 minutes**. L0glm's
ISIS fit takes **28.3 minutes**, with lower GIC, fewer false positives and lower
held-out RMSE. Biglasso's BIC minimum is the ninth of ten grid points
(`lambda=0.05690`), so the lower endpoint does not determine the result.
The [complete BIC path](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/plots/file-backed/normal-10000-1000000-lasso-path.csv)
retains every candidate's support size and score. These single-run timings
include disk access; file caching and storage speed affect them substantially.

The [comparison script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_filebacked_lasso.R)
records fitting and selection time, including common path scoring, separately
from final recovery metrics and test predictions. CV is available through the
same interface; the table reports BIC selection. Gaussian offsets and zero-weight
row exclusions are supported. Biglasso requires unrestricted coefficients;
non-unit positive weights and non-Gaussian offsets are excluded explicitly.
SIS/ISIS can also be applied to biglasso and the other `sparseGLM()` methods.

## Packed genotypes and logistic GWAS

PLINK 1 variant-major BED stores four hardcalls per byte. The native screening
kernel computes the same family-specific scores directly from these two-bit
calls, with deterministic OpenMP reduction across predictors. The selected
genotypes are decoded only for the smaller fitting problem.

This reproducible logistic example has **4,000 observations, one million
independent variants, six main effects and one pairwise interaction**.
Minor-allele frequencies range from 0.1 to 0.5, and diploid genotypes are
generated in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The BED file occupies **1 GB**, versus
32 GB for the decoded double-precision matrix. The simulator writes matching
BIM and FAM files, so the dataset can also be opened with PLINK.
The FAM file encodes controls as 1 and cases as 2; the saved R response uses 0/1.

From the checkout root, run:

```{r bed-simulate, eval=FALSE}
source("benchmarks/benchmark_filebacked_gwas.R")
results <- benchmark_filebacked_gwas(n=4000L,p=1000000L,
  cache="codex_sandbox/filebacked_gwas")
results[c("method","seconds","gic","TP","FP","FN","F1_score","MCC",
  "interaction_recovered","test_AUC","test_logloss")]
```

The [R script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_filebacked_gwas.R)
and its [small C++ simulator](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/helpers/hwe_genotypes.cpp)
contain the full simulation, including the random seeds. Packed calls are
written directly to disk, without constructing a dense genotype matrix.
For an existing BED file the fitting calls are:

```{r bed-fit, eval=FALSE}
prefix <- "codex_sandbox/filebacked_gwas/gwas-4000-1000000"
simulation <- readRDS(paste0(prefix,".rds"))
y <- simulation$response$y
offset <- simulation$response$offset
X <- l0glmData(paste0(prefix,".bed"),n=4000L,p=1000000L)
training <- seq_len(3200L)
fit <- l0glmFit(X[training,,drop=FALSE],y[training],family=binomial(),
  intercept=TRUE,offset=offset[training],screen="ISIS",screen.nthreads=8L,
  interactions=1L)
fit$interactions$history
GIC(fit)
coef(fit)[which(Matrix::rowSums(coef(fit)!=0)>0),,drop=FALSE]
predict(fit,X[3201:4000,,drop=FALSE],offset=offset[3201:4000])
```

Set `screen="SIS"` for one marginal screen and `interactions=0L` for main
effects alone. Pairwise products are generated among selected main effects;
they are stored in the model recipe and constructed only when needed.
The example deliberately includes main effects for both interacting variants.

<!-- BEGIN file-gwas-metrics -->
| Method | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | F1 | MCC | Interaction recovered | Test AUC | Test log loss |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| SIS | 3.28 | 2971 | 6 | 0 | 1 | 0.923 | 0.926 | No | 0.830 | 0.437 |
| ISIS | 7.94 | 2971 | 6 | 0 | 1 | 0.923 | 0.926 | No | 0.830 | 0.437 |
| ISIS + interactions | 10.62 | 2906 | 6 | 0 | 1 | 0.923 | 0.926 | Yes | 0.833 | 0.431 |
<!-- END file-gwas-metrics -->

The main-effect models recover all six main effects. The interaction model
retains five main effects and the true interaction, with lower GIC and held-out
log loss. Parent main effects are eligible for removal after their products
have been generated.

The first 3,200 observations train the models; 800 are held out. Recovery
includes the six main effects and the true interaction, so an omitted
interaction counts as a false negative. All rows use the same evaluation
universe: original predictors plus the union of generated interactions and
the true interaction. Simulation truth is used only for evaluation. These
independent variants provide a reproducible computational example; real GWAS
also require appropriate population-structure and relatedness adjustment.

Timings exclude generation and final metric reporting. They were measured on
an HP ZBook Fury G8 with an Intel i9-11950H, eight physical cores, 16 logical
processors and one BLAS thread. Windows may cache file reads.

PGEN uses the official [pgenlibr](https://github.com/chrchang/plink-ng/tree/master/2.0/pgenlibr)
reader, retaining continuous ALT dosages. BED coefficients count BIM allele 1;
PGEN coefficients count ALT dosage, combining ALT alleles for multiallelic records.

```{r vcf, eval=FALSE}
source <- l0glmData('variants.pgen')
source <- l0glmData('variants.vcf.gz',control=list(
  plink='C:/tools/plink2.exe',cache='C:/analysis/cache/genotypes',dosage='DS'))
```

VCF conversion uses PLINK 2 and an explicit output prefix. A provenance record
identifies the input used by a reusable cache. `dosage='DS'` preserves expected
dosages; omitting it imports GT hardcalls.

## Imputation, prediction and resampling

BED/PGEN use training-mean imputation by default; other formats require an
explicit `missing='mean'`. Only nonmissing training rows with positive weight
in at least one channel enter each mean. An all-missing column becomes zero.
Cross-validation relearns these means in each training fold. Prediction reuses
the fitted training means, including when predictor columns are reordered by
name. Bootstrap row views repeat the fitting pipeline with replicate-specific
training means.

```{r cv, eval=FALSE}
tuned <- l0glmTune(source,response,family=binomial(),tune='cv',nfolds=5L,
  nlambda=10L,screen='SIS',nsis=1000L)
predict(tuned$fit_best,source[test_rows,,drop=FALSE])
```

Keep the source files at their saved paths. File-backed intercepts can be added
with `intercept=TRUE`; existing constant columns should be named or declared
with `always.include`. Numeric starts, compulsory terms, predictor groups and
interaction terms retain their usual eligibility and screening rules.

## Streamed outcome clustering

Ward distances and cut losses add over observation blocks, so `glmCluster()` can
cluster file-backed responses without making a full dense outcome copy:

```{r cluster, eval=FALSE}
channels <- l0glmData('chromatogram.h5',dataset='intensity')
clustered <- glmCluster(channels,family=poisson(identity),linkage='ward',k.max=32L)
```

The pairwise channel distances and returned centres/aggregates must satisfy the
memory guard. Size factors use whole-channel totals, computed in a streamed
pass when omitted. Bregman agglomeration retains its bounded-matrix route.
